rows.quick: Quick answerBike fit for beginners starts with control, not a low racing position. An unfamiliar or old setup may not suit the riding you do now. Record your current position, check that you can brake safely, then compare one targeted change at a time during easy rides.
rows.article: The problem: bike fit for beginners You have bought a bike, borrowed one or taken your old bike out of storage. The first kilometres feel unfamiliar. You slide on the saddle, keep changing hand position or hold your arms rigidly. A short test ride may have felt fine, while the same position becomes uncomfortable on a longer outing. That makes starting confusing. You do not yet know what belongs to ordinary effort and what concerns the setup. Returning riders can feel uncertain too. An old position does not automatically feel comfortable after a lengthy break. You do not need to replace components immediately or copy an experienced rider's posture. Start by asking whether you can pedal, look ahead, steer and brake comfortably. This guide helps organise those first checks. Pain, tingling and lost sensation are not compulsory stages of getting used to cycling. Record when a problem starts rather than changing everything because of a vague impression. Background: getting used to a bike is not the same as fitting it Your position sits between the saddle, pedals and handlebar. Moving the saddle therefore changes more than its height alone. The distance to your hands may feel different too. One uncomfortable contact point does not immediately prove that one particular measurement is wrong. A borrowed bike still carries someone else's setup. On an old bike of your own, clothing, shoes and intended use may have changed. Perhaps you now prefer relaxed outings to fast group rides. Start with that present purpose rather than an old photograph. Frame size limits what you can adjust. Components also have their own installation limits. The Trek owner's manual, for example, warns that enough seatpost must remain inside the frame. A marking is not permission to move beyond it to reach a calculated ideal measurement. The ride itself also matters when assessing a position. A short, easy circuit is a different comparison from a demanding outing. If you ride further while adjusting components, it becomes harder to understand which change relates to your experience. Keep the first comparisons straightforward. You do not need a power meter to record your route, duration and impressions. Online tools can organise measurements and calculate an initial proposal. They cannot observe your braking or movement when you become tired. They do not investigate pain either. Ask a mechanic about uncertain installation and a fitter about persistent positioning difficulties. Medical symptoms belong with a clinician. These boundaries do not make a basic starting measurement less useful; they make its meaning clearer. How to approach it with bike fitting Make the bike safe first: Check tyres, brakes and component security according to the manufacturer's instructions. Do not use a ride to discover whether a loose handlebar will stay attached. Ask a mechanic if installation is uncertain. Check that you can operate the brakes from your normal hand position without sliding forwards on the saddle. Keep the starting position: Stand the bike upright on a level floor. Use a tape measure for saddle height. Measure from the centre of the bottom bracket to a consistent point on the saddle. Record that point and the measurement in millimetres. Take a side photograph and record saddle and handlebar positions so you can recover the original setup later. Calculate an initial comparison: Measure your body using the instructions in the bike fit calculator. Check the units and repeat any uncertain measurement. Treat the result as a proposal rather than a compulsory final position. A large difference from your current setup calls for checking the inputs and measurement method before making a change. Choose one understandable adjustment: Work only on a component that you know how to adjust safely. Record the old and new measurements, including the direction. No fixed millimetre step suits every beginner and every component. Remain within manufacturer limits and use the specified tools. Let a professional adjust an unfamiliar handlebar or saddle assembly instead. Compare two to three easy rides: Use a familiar route and similar effort while you remain symptom-free. Record whether pedalling, braking and looking ahead become easier. Note new pressure points too; a better saddle sensation is not the whole result. Return to the recorded safe position if things worsen. Do not finish a testing series at the expense of pain. Recognise the limit of self-testing: Stop for lost sensation, radiating tingling or symptoms that reduce your control of the bike. Seek medical assessment for pain at rest or at night, swelling or persistent symptoms. If pain remains after three to four careful adjustments, consult a fitter and, where appropriate, a clinician. A new bike is never a reason to ignore warning signs while trying to settle into cycling. Further reading Bike fit and body proportions explains why a friend of the same height does not provide a reliable personal starting position. Bike frame size helps check whether the bike offers enough adjustment room for your riding position. Saddle height expands the first saddle measurement before you start changing other contact points. Handlebar width and hood position helps assess safe hand contact without immediately buying a different handlebar. Cycling power and pacing helps keep effort during comparison rides deliberate and straightforward to record. The bike fit calculator gathers your body measurements and offers an initial proposal to assess on the bike. Frequently asked questions Do I need special cycling shoes for my first setup? No. Record the shoes and pedals you currently use and compare your first rides with those. Different shoes can change the starting conditions. Recheck your position when you switch rather than changing shoes, saddle and handlebar together. You do not need a complete new equipment collection to investigate one unclear discomfort. Can I use my old saddle position when returning to cycling? You can record it as a starting point if the installation is safe. It does not prove that the same position still suits your current rides. Start gently and check brake access, pedalling and comfort again. Change something only when you have a clear reason and a safe way to compare it. Should I always reach the ground with both feet flat? Do not use that as the only measure of saddle height. The bike type and how you mount and dismount also matter. Ask for help if stopping feels uncertain. You need to stop and get off safely, but saddle position must also be assessed while you pedal. Is a free calculation enough before I attempt longer rides? A calculation is a beginning, not a declaration that everything is correct. Check the proposal during easy rides and build experience with your own bike. Ask for help if the position remains uncertain or symptoms develop. acceptedAnswer.text: You can record it as a starting point if the installation is safe. It does not prove that the same position still suits your current rides. h1: Numb toes cycling: pressure and shoe fit
rows.quick: Quick answerNumb toes cycling often starts with pressure you only notice during a ride. First check whether your shoe has enough room and the fastening is not tight. Avoid changing your entire position immediately: compare one small adjustment at a time and ask a clinician about recurring or lasting numbness.
rows.article: The problem: numb toes cycling Your shoes feel comfortable at home. On the road, a burning sensation develops beneath the forefoot. Your toes tingle or feel less distinct. Loosening the shoe may help briefly, but the problem returns later. Notice exactly where you feel it. Is the pressure on top, along the outer edge or beneath the ball? Does it start in both feet together? Differences between your feet may matter more than the size printed on the box. Record when it happens too. Is it linked to warmth, long climbs or harder pedalling? Are you wearing different socks from those used when fitting the shoes? A shoe that feels pleasant when walking need not provide the same support while cycling. You need not wait until your whole foot becomes numb. Stop loading it when tingling develops and check the pressure. Bike position cannot explain every foot symptom. Include symptoms away from the bike in your notes. Background: space, pressure and foot support Your foot sits between an insole, an upper and a fairly stiff outer sole. The fastening keeps it in place. Excessive tension can create local pressure. Tightening further therefore cannot automatically correct an unsuitable shoe shape. Length and width are different measurements. A longer shoe may still be too narrow at the forefoot. Conversely, an oversized shoe may let your foot slide. You might then tighten the fastening harder to compensate for that movement. Cleats connect the foot to the pedal. Their position changes where support is felt beneath the shoe. Moving them backwards can be a trial for forefoot pressure, but does not prove they caused it. Rotation and available movement also matter. An insole occupies space. A thicker replacement can therefore create a new pressure spot. Compare changes to the insole, sock and fastening separately. Avoid buying more support immediately when the shoe already feels cramped. Bike position affects the whole arrangement. Reaching for the pedals may change how you load the foot. However, a burning forefoot does not reliably prove that the saddle is too high. Checking the shoe first avoids unrelated adjustments elsewhere. An online photograph cannot assess sensation, circulation or nerve function. The pattern of symptoms remains important. The NHS guidance on pins and needles advises medical assessment for recurring or persistent symptoms. Use a calculator for dimensions, not diagnosis. How to approach it with bike fitting Record your starting point. Photograph both cleats directly from below. Mark their outlines with removable tape. Note your shoes, socks, insoles and when the problem starts. Record the pressure location for each foot. This makes a later comparison more useful than relying on memory alone. Check shoe space first. Use the socks you normally ride in. Check that the toes have room without the heel lifting freely. Look for pressure along the forefoot edge. A visible mark is a clue, not a diagnosis. Ask a shop or fitter to compare shoe shapes when uncertain. Reduce unnecessary fastening pressure. Loosen slightly without letting the foot slide. Check for a folded tongue or sock. Choose a short, easy ride close to home. Stop if numbness returns. Do not continue simply to complete a planned testing duration. Comfort should not depend on ignoring reduced sensation. Only then consider the cleat. For local forefoot pressure, discuss a small backward trial, for example 2–3 mm. This is a cautious fitting trial, not medical treatment. Stay within the slots and follow the specified tightening torque. Do not change rotation simultaneously. Get help if you cannot check the attachment safely. Compare one change over 2–3 easy rides. Keep shoes, socks and route reasonably similar. Record whether pressure starts later, reduces or moves elsewhere. Return to the mark if a new problem appears. Numbness is not a reason to wait several rides before seeking help. Check the wider position. Discuss persistent differences between feet with a fitter. Use the bike fit calculator below only for a first check of your overall position. Avoid moving the saddle randomly to address shoe pressure. Take your notes and photographs to an assessment. Warning signs: stop for numbness or increasing pain. Ask a clinician about symptoms at rest, night pain, swelling or radiating tingling. Continuing to guess after 3–4 careful adjustments is unhelpful. Persistent numbness warrants earlier medical assessment; a bike fitter cannot replace that assessment. Further reading Road bike fit: your three contact points explains how shoe, pedal and seated position interact without assigning one symptom to one measurement. Bike setup measurements: record your position helps you document a clear baseline before making a change. Lower back pain cycling: check your position calmly discusses symptoms that may extend beyond local shoe pressure. Bike fit calculator provides a starting position to compare with your measurements, not a diagnosis of foot pain. Frequently asked questions Should I buy cycling shoes one size larger? Not automatically. Compare length, forefoot width and space above the foot first. A larger size may allow sliding while the pressure edge remains. Take your riding socks when trying shoes. Compare different shoe shapes rather than increasing the size alone. Can I test without cleats? That may change the loading, but also changes several variables together. It is not conclusive evidence about the cause. Make sure the shoes and pedals work safely together. Never leave cleat bolts loose as an improvised way of allowing more movement. Why does loosening help only briefly? Fastening pressure may contribute while shoe shape or the insole also matters. Temporary relief does not identify the main cause. Record where pressure returns. If tingling continues after stopping, seek medical assessment instead of repeatedly making the shoe looser and continuing the ride. Must both cleats have identical positions? Feet do not always share the same shape. Avoid copying millimetres without checking placement. Record each starting position separately. Record the pressure location for each foot. This makes a later comparison more useful than relying on memory alone. Check shoe space first. Use the socks you normally ride in. Check that the toes have room without the heel lifting freely. Look for pressure along the forefoot edge. A visible mark is a clue, not a diagnosis. Ask a shop or fitter to compare shoe shapes when uncertain. Reduce unnecessary fastening pressure. Loosen slightly without letting the foot slide. Check for a folded tongue or sock. Choose a short, easy ride close to home. Stop if numbness returns. Do not continue simply to complete a planned testing duration. Comfort should not depend on ignoring reduced sensation. Only then consider the cleat. For local forefoot pressure, discuss a small backward trial, for example 2–3 mm. This is a cautious fitting trial, not medical treatment. Stay within the slots and follow the specified tightening torque. Do not change rotation simultaneously. Get help if you cannot check the attachment safely. Compare one change over 2–3 easy rides. Keep shoes, socks and route reasonably similar. Record whether pressure starts later, reduces or moves elsewhere. Return to the mark if a new problem appears. Numbness is not a reason to wait several rides before seeking help. Check the wider position. Discuss persistent differences between feet with a fitter. Use the bike fit calculator below only for a first check of your overall position. Avoid moving the saddle randomly to address shoe pressure. Take your notes and photographs to an assessment. Warning signs: stop for numbness or increasing pain. Ask a clinician about symptoms at rest, night pain, swelling or radiating tingling. Continuing to guess after 3–4 careful adjustments is unhelpful. Persistent numbness warrants earlier medical assessment; a bike fitter cannot replace that assessment.

h1: Numb hands cycling: where should you start?
rows.quick: Quick answerWith numb hands cycling, pressure through your hands and your wrist position may play a part. Start by recording when symptoms appear and checking whether you can reach the brake hoods comfortably. Do not keep riding through numbness; symptoms that persist or return need assessment.
rows.article: The problem: numb hands cycling Your fingers begin tingling during a long ride. Perhaps you only notice it on the brake hoods. Your hand feels better in the drops, or exactly the opposite happens. Sometimes you mainly feel pressure beneath your palm. Sometimes your wrist hurts when you brake. Those differences provide useful information. Record which hand and which fingers are affected. Note where you held the bar and when symptoms began. Was it on smooth roads, gravel or a descent? Symptoms that appear immediately need a different discussion from discomfort after an unusually long ride. You do not need to diagnose yourself. Numbness is not a normal price to pay for a sporting position. Thick gloves may change the sensation, but they do not explain why you lean so heavily on the bars. This guide helps you examine your setup systematically. Have symptoms assessed if they persist. Background: pressure, wrist position and handlebar reach Your hands steer, brake and carry part of the load. How that feels depends on several components. Consider handlebar distance, the shape of the brake hoods and your position on the saddle. Fatigue and vibration also change how firmly you grip the bars. Distant bars may encourage you to straighten your elbows. Your wrist may then bend backwards. Higher bars do not automatically mean less hand pressure. If you slide forwards on the saddle, the load keeps changing. Look at the whole position before buying a different stem. The brake hoods are important contact surfaces themselves. Their angle and location affect how your hand rests on them. A hood that feels pleasant while stationary may be less usable under braking. You need to operate the brake lever safely without holding your hand at an awkward angle. According to British Cycling on hand and wrist discomfort, local pressure can accompany tingling and numbness. That does not establish the cause in your case. Gloves, bar tape, road surfaces and previous symptoms can also matter. Symptoms away from cycling are relevant too. A photograph shows your position at one moment. It cannot measure pressure or tell you how your hand feels later. A calculator cannot identify which structure is sensitive either. Use online information to prepare a focused question. Then compare your experience during an easy ride, rather than judging only how the bike looks. How to approach it with bike fitting Record your starting point: Stand your bike upright and photograph the bars from the side. Use a tape measure to record the distance from the saddle nose to a fixed point on the hood, in millimetres. Also record stem length and spacer height. Use exactly the same measuring points next time. Record symptoms separately; a distance is not a comfort score. Check your reach without loosening anything: Hold the hoods as you would during an easy ride. Check whether your fingers can reach the brake levers comfortably. See whether your wrist roughly follows your forearm. Do not force your wrist straight while tightening your shoulders. Ask someone to take a side photograph while you stand safely. Separate possible causes: If pressure mainly appears on rough surfaces, record that alongside tyre pressure and gloves. If you keep sliding forwards, include saddle position in your discussion. Use the bike fit calculator to organise your starting measurements. Its result is a starting point for checking your position, not a treatment for numbness. Choose one small, reversible change: There is no safe standard correction of a particular number of degrees for every wrist. Ask a fitter whether hood position, bar height or handlebar distance deserves attention first. Record the agreed change in millimetres or degrees and keep a record of the old position. Follow the component manual and specified torque during assembly; have uncertain mechanical work done by a professional. Test within clear limits: Compare one change over two to three easy, similar rides, provided you remain symptom-free. Keep the route, gloves and effort as consistent as possible. Record when discomfort appears and whether braking and steering stay normal. Stop when numbness or pain develops; the testing schedule is not a reason to keep riding. If things worsen, return to the safely recorded starting position and seek help. Recognise when adjustment is not enough: Discuss persistent or recurring numbness with a clinician. That also applies to weakness, radiating tingling, swelling or pain at rest or during the night. If ordinary position-related pain persists after three to four careful adjustments, consult a fitter and, where appropriate, a clinician. Do not wait for all those adjustments before seeking help for lost sensation. Further reading Stem length explains how to measure handlebar distance without using saddle position as a quick workaround. Gravel bike fit helps you assess hand position and reach on surfaces that create more vibration. Saddle pain cycling: support, pressure and friction discusses why saddle support also affects your position on the bars. Online bike fit limitations helps you choose between measuring yourself and arranging a supervised assessment. The bike fit calculator brings your measurements together so you can prepare for your next position check. Frequently asked questions Should I buy different gloves immediately? That does not have to be your first step. Record where pressure develops and how your hands rest on the hoods. You can compare gloves on a short, easy ride. Do not use extra padding to tolerate numbness. Changing equipment alone is insufficient when symptoms keep returning. Is a shorter stem always better for my hands? No. A shorter stem changes your reach, but does not automatically address the cause of hand pressure. Hood position and support on the saddle matter too. Have the proposed change assessed, then check steering as well. A small change in distance may feel different from what you expect. Can I simply move my hands more often? Changing hand positions regularly can feel pleasant during normal rides, provided you can brake and steer safely. It does not resolve persistent lost sensation. If you constantly move to suppress symptoms, record that pattern. Discuss recurring numbness with a clinician and your position with a fitter. What should I bring to a fitter or clinician? Bring notes about the location, duration and circumstances of your symptoms. Add photographs and your original setup measurements. Mention symptoms away from cycling or any loss of strength. rows.quick: Quick answerNeck pain cycling can relate to prolonged upward looking, excessive reaching or tense shoulders. Perhaps the tension sits where your neck meets your shoulder. Or you have to tilt your head far back to see the road ahead. Record when it starts and where you feel it. Separate local tiredness from sharp pain or tingling down an arm. Note whether it affects the left side, right side or both. This gives you more useful information than simply saying the bike feels too long. Compare an easy ride with a faster group outing. Symptoms that remain after dismounting need consideration beyond bike settings. Background Your neck connects your torso to your view of the road. As your torso moves lower, your head often turns further upward. More handlebar drop can therefore feel acceptable to your legs but demanding for your neck. A low position is not a goal in itself. A long distance to the brake hoods may straighten your elbows. Your shoulders then move forward or upward to reach the bars. A cramped position can also feel uncomfortable. Stem length alone cannot establish whether the complete position suits you or explains a particular symptom. Your saddle establishes the starting point of your pelvis. You also change pelvic support and your relationship to the pedals when you do this. Load away from cycling matters too. Also note whether you slide forwards and when this starts. Compare more than the sensation in your arms alone. Check whether you can brake directly and safely from your usual seated position without having to move your hands first. Separate saddle checks from handlebar checks: Record your current saddle height and seated position with a tape measure and side photograph. Measure in millimetres from fixed reference points. Note where on the saddle you normally sit. Use the bike fit calculator for an initial body-measurement comparison, but do not automatically slide the saddle forwards when hand distance differs considerably. Measure the actual hand position: With the bike upright, measure from a fixed saddle point to your usual supporting hand position. Record the height difference too and take a photograph showing both reference points. This measurement helps track your own adjustments. It is not a universal target that you need to share with any other particular rider. A higher saddle increases the distance you need to reach near the bottom. A lower saddle reduces that distance. That alone does not tell you which position suits you. Your foot is another contact point. A different sole, pedal or cleat can change the relationship between your foot and bike. Comparing saddle height alone may therefore miss an important difference. Record which shoes and pedals you used with that measurement. A familiar rule immediately links pain at the front to a low saddle. That association is not a reliable personal diagnosis. Pain location does not justify a fixed correction of several millimetres either. Without assessing your movement and symptoms, the explanation remains uncertain. Riding load belongs in the same discussion. Consider a new route, more climbing or a different gear. A fall, previous injury and symptoms while walking also matter to a clinician. A fitter can assess your cycling position but cannot replace medical assessment. A stationary photograph shows only one moment. It cannot show how much riding load your knee can tolerate. A calculator cannot diagnose the problem either. Use its output as a measurement reference and discuss large differences before adopting them. The aim is a comparison you can evaluate, not a number you must achieve despite pain.

sections.title: How to approach it with bike fitting
sections.text: Start with a symptom record: Note which knee hurts and where you feel discomfort. Write down the activity, when symptoms begin and any recent changes. Include pain while walking, resting or sleeping. Stop the ride when pain appears; a test is not an instruction to provoke symptoms. Keep your starting position: Hold the bike upright and take a clear side photograph. Use a tape measure from the centre of the bottom bracket to the same point on the saddle top. Record that distance in millimetres, alongside your shoes, pedals and saddle rail position. Mark the original seatpost position with removable tape without covering safety markings. Check what actually changed: Compare your notes with the previous comfortable setup. Remember shoe soles, cleats and riding load too. Do not change saddle height, setback and cleats together. Ask a mechanic to check component security if you are unsure about it. Use a calculation as a discussion point: Enter your measured inseam in the saddle height calculator. Compare its starting recommendation with your measurement. A difference does not explain knee pain or justify a large adjustment. When symptoms are present, discuss which single change makes sense with a fitter first. A comparison of, for example, 2–3 mm of saddle height is small and reversible, not a treatment or fixed recommendation. Test within clear limits: If there is no reason for medical assessment first, compare one agreed change. Use two to three easy, comparable rides only while you remain symptom-free. Keep shoes, route and effort as consistent as possible. Record the difference and restore the safely recorded original position if things worsen. Follow component instructions and tightening torque during installation. Recognise warning signs: Seek urgent medical assessment for sudden severe pain, inability to bear weight, major swelling or a locking knee. The same applies to a hot, red knee with fever, as described in NHS knee pain advice. Contact a clinician for pain at rest, night pain or radiating tingling. If mild symptoms remain after three to four careful adjustments, involve a fitter and clinician; do not wait through that sequence when warning signs occur.

Cleat position explains which foot settings to record before making a careful comparison. Pedal stance width explains why lateral space cannot be inferred from pain location alone. Bike fit for beginners helps you consider setup and a gradual return to riding separately. The saddle height calculator provides a measurement reference rather than an explanation or treatment for knee pain.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions
sections.text: A video can show what you do while pedalling. Record it safely without provoking pain. It cannot diagnose a condition or measure the load inside your knee. Bring it as additional information, alongside your symptom history and the changes you have made to the bike. A matching starting position is easy to record, but does not prove both feet need exactly the same setting. Do not rotate one cleat solely because one knee hurts. Have foot position, available movement and safe operation considered together before trying to correct an apparent difference. Do not treat a setup experiment as permission to train through pain. Record which activities cause symptoms and discuss your next steps with a clinician if pain persists. A fitter can help assess your riding position but cannot remotely determine which training load is medically appropriate for you. Bring your bike, normal cycling shoes and original measurements. Add symptom notes and recent changes. Explain whether walking or sleeping also causes pain. Mention earlier injuries and what happened after each adjustment; this helps the assessment start with useful information rather than random changes to the bicycle. h1: Lower back pain cycling: check your position calmly
rows.quick: Quick answerLower back pain cycling calls for a description of your symptoms before choosing another stem. A position requiring uncomfortable reaching or bending can be a reason to check your setup. Record your current measurements, change one thing at a time, and have persistent or concerning symptoms assessed rather than explaining them from the bike alone.
rows.article: The problem: lower back pain cycling Your back feels uncomfortable when you spend longer on the hoods. Perhaps you keep shifting on the saddle or sitting upright. You want to know whether the distance to the bars is right. At the same time, you cannot tell whether the bike explains everything. Start with the circumstances. Is the feeling in the middle of your lower back or more to one side? Does it appear during easy riding, climbing or a low position? Also record whether it disappears after dismounting or remains present. A new bike, longer ride or changed bar position provides a clear comparison point. Sometimes nothing on the bike has changed. Write that down too, without choosing your own explanation. Your notes help a fitter or clinician ask more focused questions. You do not need to provoke the symptom again for a useful description. Use what you have already observed on previous rides. Background: assess seating and reach together Your hands, saddle and pedals determine where you find support. Changing a contact point also changes the position between those points. More distant bars require greater reach from your seat. A larger height difference can change the position of your torso. That makes a handlebar measurement relevant, but does not establish a cause of back pain. Two riders can experience identical measurements very differently. The same person can also experience a position differently during a longer or harder ride. A measurement describes your bike; it does not provide a diagnosis. First consider whether your seating remains stable. If you keep sliding forwards, you are not always measuring from the same position. Moving the saddle forwards shortens reach, but also changes your position relative to the pedals. That makes the influence of the bars harder to assess separately. A side photograph can help you recover your starting position. It does not show how you move throughout an entire ride. Nor can a back shape tell you why someone has pain. A fitter can assess movement alongside the bike; medical questions belong with a clinician. Include the course of your rides too. A changed training week, unusual effort or prolonged use of one hand position may matter for comparison. You do not need to label any of those as a separate cause. Aim for an honest overview before identifying a component as the solution. How to approach it with bike fitting Make a short symptom record. Note location, starting point, hand position and ride type. Include what happened after you stopped. Use existing observations; do not continue riding to make a symptom measurable. For pain at rest or other warning signs, skip the self-test and seek medical assessment. Record the starting setup. Place the bike level and use a tape measure and spirit level. Note saddle height, saddle position, bar height difference and distance to the hood. Name the reference points and take a side photograph. Check for shifted or loose components too; resolve uncertain installation before riding. Look at seating before changing reach. Can you remain in the same place without sliding forwards? Ask a fitter to observe if that is unclear. Use the bike fit calculator to organise your measurements. A difference from its calculation does not prove that measurement causes your back symptoms. Choose one small, focused comparison. If bar height difference seems particularly difficult to use, discuss a permitted increase. A 2–5 mm step can be a cautious comparison example. It is not a prescribed treatment, and not every system allows that step. Respect manufacturer limits, cable clearance and torque settings; have a mechanic check installation. Compare without collecting pain. Leave the saddle, shoes and other bar settings unchanged. First check braking and steering in a safe place. Then try two to three easy rides while you remain symptom-free. Keep route and effort comparable, and record whether the position becomes easier to use. Return or seek help. Stop for new or increasing pain and restore the recorded safe starting setup, with help if necessary. Feeling better while stationary is insufficient reason to ride through symptoms. Have pain persisting after three to four careful adjustments assessed by a fitter and a clinician where appropriate. Pain at rest, night pain, swelling and radiating tingling need earlier medical assessment. Do not wait for another adjustment attempt. New loss of sensation also means stopping the comparison and seeking assessment. You do not first need to prove that the bike caused the symptom. New loss of sensation around your groin or loss of bladder or bowel control needs immediate emergency assessment. Back pain with pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs also needs emergency help. See the medical warning signs for back pain; do not wait for a bike fitting appointment. Endurance bike fit: comfort over distance explains how to compare duration and position separately during easy rides. No, you have a useful observation about that position. It can inform the next assessment, but does not fully explain the symptom. Record when things feel better and what stayed the same. Share that information with a fitter or clinician if symptoms return or persist over time. Can I use an old bike for comparison? Yes, when it remains safe and comfortable to use. Measure the same contact points on both bikes. Record differences in saddle shape and brake hoods too, because equal distances can feel different. rows.title: Bike size and geometry | BestBikeFit4U
rows.description: Unsure about bike size and geometry? Compare stack, reach and adjustment room with your current bike. Learn which measurements to check before choosing.
rows.keywordMeta: bike size and geometry,stack and reach,compare frame sizes,bike adjustment range
rows.quick: Quick answerBike size and geometry together tell you more than a frame's size label. Start with your current bike's stack and reach, then record how its saddle and bars are set up. Compare a candidate against that baseline, including permitted adjustment room; a suitable size label does not guarantee a suitable riding position.
rows.article: The problem: comparing bike size and geometry You currently ride a medium, but another brand suggests a size 54. A sizing chart puts you exactly between two options. Meanwhile, someone says a smaller bike is always more sporting. That makes the decision unnecessarily confusing when you mainly want to ride comfortably. A size label is a useful description within a model range. It does not describe every distance you experience on the bike. Even two bikes with the same label on their seat tubes can feel different. The fitted components change things further. Perhaps your current bike feels good and you want to transfer that position. Perhaps you want less distance to the bars instead. Make that goal clear first. Otherwise, you compare numbers without knowing which difference you need. This guide helps you prepare a comparison so a test ride or discussion with a fitter becomes more focused. Background: what stack and reach tell you Stack is the vertical distance between the bottom bracket and the top of the head tube. Reach is the horizontal distance between those same reference points. They describe the frame independently of a sloping top tube. Always check the manufacturer's measurement definition, especially with integrated components. Your hand position sits further along. Spacers, stem, bar shape and brake hoods add to the frame dimensions. A frame with identical reach can therefore produce a different hand reach. Stack is not the same as handlebar height either. Compare the complete build when transferring an existing riding position. At the rear, saddle height, seatpost and setback matter. Seat tube angle affects where the seatpost sits. The saddle rails have a limited adjustment range. Use that range to position your seat, not to hide an unsuitable handlebar distance. Standover height and clearance above the top tube are separate measurements. They help you check practical use of the bike. Shoe clearance, tyre clearance and intended riding also deserve attention. No single ratio proves that the entire package is suitable. Online information can make those differences visible on paper. It cannot tell you whether operating the controls feels comfortable on a descent. A suitable stem also needs to be available and permitted. Treat a calculated frame size as a selection aid. Your final choice needs a check of the bike as you will actually use it. How to approach it with bike fitting Describe your starting point: Record your current bike's brand, model, model year and size. Write down what feels good and what you want to change. Use concrete observations such as reaching, sliding forwards or difficult braking. Keep a side photograph of the whole bike. A size label without its model year is insufficient for a reliable comparison. Collect the official geometry: Find stack and reach in the table for that exact size and version. Record millimetres and retain the measurement definition. Do the same for each candidate. Do not use a chart for an almost identical model. Check whether a listed dimension describes the frame or the complete bar position. Measure your contact points: Stand the bike upright on level ground and use a tape measure and spirit level. Record saddle height from the bottom bracket. Measure bar height and horizontal distance using consistent reference points. Also record stem length, spacers and bar shape. Repeat uncertain measurements before drawing conclusions from a small difference. Check adjustment room: Ask which stems, seatposts and spacers are permitted on the candidate. Compare minimum and maximum markings in the component instructions. Do not rely on a future modification outside those limits. Use the frame size calculator as another starting point alongside these details, not as a replacement for checking them. Compare the built bike: Have a candidate safely adjusted to the agreed starting position. Change one setting at a time and record the difference in millimetres. Comparing models is not a reason to cut components immediately. If you can borrow the bike, compare two to three easy rides in similar conditions, provided you remain symptom-free. Assess the result and its limits: Check reach, braking, steering and seating, rather than just how low the bars sit. If things worsen, return to the recorded safe position. Ask a fitter for help if you repeatedly reach adjustment limits. Seek medical assessment for pain at rest or during the night, swelling or radiating tingling. If position-related pain persists after three to four careful adjustments, seek guidance; do not wait that long with lost sensation. Further reading Race versus endurance geometry helps you compare the intended riding position without relying only on a sales category. Stem length explains why frame reach and the distance to your hands are different measurements. Crank length discusses a component that changes your pedalling movement without changing frame size. Online bike fit limitations helps you decide when measurements on paper provide insufficient confidence. The frame size calculator gives you a starting selection, after which you check geometry and adjustment room separately. Frequently asked questions Can I use my current size label with another brand? Use it only as an initial search direction. Then check model year, geometry and fitted components. A size label has no fixed universal meaning. Compare your current contact points with the possible build of the new bike. That compares the position you will ride, rather than just its label. Is the smaller option better when I fall between sizes? You cannot establish that from a sizing chart alone. The smaller option may offer different bar height and adjustment room. The larger one may start too long. Compare both complete builds and seek guidance if either option immediately puts you at an adjustment limit. Are identical stack and reach enough for the same position? No. Stem, spacers, bar shape and brake hoods help determine where your hands land. Saddle position also needs to match. Identical frame dimensions simplify the comparison but cannot replace checking your contact points. Remember that the chosen components must also be installed within their permitted limits. A size label is a useful description within a model range. It does not describe every distance you experience on the bike. Even two bikes with the same label on their seat tubes can feel different. The fitted components change things further.

Perhaps your current bike feels good and you want to transfer that position. Perhaps you want less distance to the bars instead. Make that goal clear first. Otherwise, you compare numbers without knowing which difference you need.

rows.description: How many carbohydrates should you carry on a ride? Use duration, product labels and experience to build a practical plan. Practise eating on easy rides.

h1: Carbs per hour cycling: make your plan
rows.quick: Quick answerCarbs per hour cycling depends on duration, effort and what your stomach tolerates. The calculator uses Jeukendrup’s duration categories as a starting point and displays upper amounts, not a compulsory quota. Add food and carbohydrate in drinks together, then practise a workable plan before relying on it during an important ride.
rows.article: The problem: carbs per hour cycling You carry gels, a banana and sports drink but do not know their combined carbohydrate amount. On one ride you wait until you feel empty before eating. On another you consume everything close together. Neither situation clearly reveals which plan you tolerate well or can repeat comfortably. An hourly amount helps compare preparation with experience. It is different from counting how many packets fit in a jersey pocket. Products vary in serving size and composition. A full bottle may contain carbohydrate or none at all, depending on what you actually mix into the water. Begin with an ordinary ride you know well. Record duration, effort and what you really consume. Note when eating becomes difficult because of pace, terrain, packaging or stomach comfort. A plan only works when its execution on the bicycle is practical, rather than merely looking tidy on paper. Background The calculator follows the approved categories from Jeukendrup 2014. Below half an hour, carbohydrate during the ride is unnecessary. Advice up to an hour remains small and qualitative. The tool then uses up to 30, 60 or 90 grams per hour according to duration; the highest category requires multiple carbohydrate sources. These values do not instruct you to reach the maximum every time. Intensity, opportunities to eat and tolerance remain important. A short easy outing calls for different preparation from a prolonged effort. Previous meals also provide context, although the calculator does not assess your entire day's dietary intake or individual clinical needs. Read labels per serving and per packet. One packet may contain several servings. For drinks, consider the actual quantity of powder in your bottle. Water with a tablet does not automatically contain as much carbohydrate as an energy drink. Count what the label on that particular product specifies. Solid food, gels and drinks are practical ways to implement the plan. Choice partly depends on access and preference. You do not need to obtain everything from one product. When testing, change one element rather than replacing brand, concentration, quantity and riding pace at the same time. Body mass is not a reason to multiply the displayed amount automatically. The tool provides a duration-based starting point rather than individual nutritional treatment. If you have a medical condition or prescribed diet, discuss your plan with an appropriate professional rather than following a calculation without considering that context. How to approach it Choose the expected duration of your next ride. Use a realistic time, including easier sections. Enter it into the nutrition tool and read the accompanying explanation. Record the upper amount and the type of guidance. Do not turn qualitative advice for a short ride into an invented exact hourly carbohydrate target. List the carbohydrate in your chosen products. Use the label on the actual packet and the drink you really mix. Add those quantities together. Divide the total by planned hours to review your own plan. This reveals mistakes such as counting the same carbohydrate both as a complete drink and as a separate serving. Distribute food across practical opportunities. Choose calm, visible sections of the route and use a reminder if useful. Open packaging beforehand when safe and practical. Stop briefly if opening or eating affects steering control. Following a precise timetable matters less than being able to brake and respond safely to what happens around you. Start with products and amounts previously tolerated. Then test one change over two or three easy rides. Record stomach comfort, execution and leftovers. Do not immediately add more products after symptoms simply to reach a theoretical maximum. Return to a previously tolerated plan and examine what changed before attempting a different approach. Check the relationship with drinks. Bottle carbohydrate contributes to nutrition, but fluid needs are a separate consideration. Do not arbitrarily strengthen a drink to carry less volume. Follow product instructions and keep concentration repeatable. Plan a stop when the route requires more supplies than you can carry safely and comfortably on your bicycle. Use ride notes to refine the plan, not just the calculator's final number. Stop and seek help for feeling seriously unwell, confusion or persistent vomiting. Pain at rest, night pain or swelling needs clinical attention. Have recurrent symptoms assessed by a sports dietitian or clinician; a fitter can help when eating mainly disrupts posture or control. Further reading Cycling fueling basics: build a practical plan turns the calculation into accessible food and suitable opportunities on the road. Sodium cycling drink: read the concentration explains why carbohydrate and sodium are separate pieces of label information. Cycling watts per kilogram: understand the number puts effort into context without linking food solely to riding speed. The fuel and hydration calculator displays the duration category, total amount and limitations of its guidance for your planned outing. Frequently asked questions Must I always consume the displayed maximum? No. The tool shows an upper amount within a selected duration category, not a compulsory intake for every ride. Read the explanation and consider previous tolerance. Easier efforts may require less. Make your plan practical before attempting to reach a larger number simply because it is displayed. Does carbohydrate in sports drink count? Yes, include the amount in the drink actually mixed alongside food. Use product information and your mixing quantity. A bottle of plain water contributes no carbohydrate. Avoid double counting when recording both the total content of a bottle and the individual servings of powder used to prepare it. Can I carry only bananas? Choice depends on duration, carrying space and tolerance. A banana does not provide a fixed packet value like a measured product. That makes planning less precise, not automatically wrong. Practise carrying and eating your food, and consider the explanation accompanying higher intake categories when preparing longer rides. What if my stomach does not tolerate the plan? Do not keep consuming extra just to complete the schedule. Reduce effort, stop if necessary and review the last approach you tolerated well. Persistent or severe symptoms need professional assessment. A calculator cannot determine why your stomach reacts or exclude a medical problem from the information entered.Turn expected ride duration into a practical starting point for food and drink.Plan my fuel and hydration

rows.quick: Quick answerCleat position starts with a shoe that fits and a secure connection to your pedal. If your foot feels forced or your heel touches the crank, inspect the existing installation and record your starting point. Then change only one direction at a time; one fixed position does not suit every rider.
rows.article: The problem: finding your cleat position You clip in and notice that your foot does not feel comfortable on the pedal. Perhaps your heel wants to move outward. h1: Cycling climb time: plan your effort
rows.quick: Quick answerEstimating your cycling climb time starts with distance, average gradient, body mass and a usable FTP estimate. The calculator combines these with fixed assumptions about your bike and resistance; wind, stops and steep sections can change your actual time. Treat the result as preparation and check your effort during easy practice rides.
rows.article: The problem: estimating cycling climb time You are planning a hilly ride and want to know when you will reach the top. The distance looks manageable, but the elevation profile leaves you unsure. Perhaps you still have further to ride afterwards. A fast first climb is not automatically a good start. On previous rides, you may have started too hard. A steeper section forced you to push a heavy gear or stand. Your expected arrival time kept slipping. A calculation can then create pressure instead of clarity. Comparing yourself with a riding partner does not always help. Your mass, bikes, positions and available power differ. An average gradient also cannot describe every change along the climb. A steady road differs from alternating steep and flat sections. This guide helps you interpret an estimate and check it practically. You do not need a record attempt. The aim is a workable starting point, allowing for traffic, conditions and personal experience. Background: what the calculation includes The climb calculator uses distance and average gradient. You also enter body mass, bike type and FTP. Here, FTP provides a power reference, not proof that you can sustain it everywhere. The calculation selects a power factor using a distance category. That is a simplification. A short, steep climb can take longer than a longer, shallow climb. The distance category therefore measures neither your capacity nor the actual duration directly. Do not treat the suggested power as an instruction. The physics model adds resistance from climbing, rolling and air. It also accounts for drivetrain losses. Body mass and a default bike mass together form the total mass. The chosen bike type also supplies fixed assumptions about aerodynamic resistance and surface. There is no personal measurement of your position. Wind is not entered separately. A headwind can change your actual speed without the calculator knowing. Luggage, road conditions and stops may also differ from the assumptions. Calculated time comes from distance divided by estimated speed. This assumes a steady situation. It does not predict braking, corners or transitions between sitting and standing. A reliable time is unavailable outside the calculation range. A suitable position helps you control the bike and assess your effort. It does not guarantee a time saving. Online tools let you compare inputs, but cannot establish your personal limit for sustained exercise. Keep the calculation alongside your ride notes, rather than giving it priority over them. How to approach it: from estimate to practice ride Check the route profile: Record the climb length and the source of its average gradient. Look for the steeper sections too. Keep distance in kilometres and gradient in percent to avoid mixing units. Plan a safe route back and allow for breaks. An arrival time must never decide whether you continue in unsafe conditions. Record your inputs: Use current body mass and a recent FTP estimate with a known origin. Record how that value was obtained. Choose the closest bike type and remember that its mass is a default value. Use the climb calculator to record your starting point. Consider carried luggage when assessing uncertainty in the result. Compare assumptions: First change only FTP to another value supported by your own records. Check the effect on time and power. Then consider changing gradient if your route information supports a different value. Do not select a favourable number to obtain a desired finish time. This comparison shows sensitivity to assumptions, not an individual training prescription. Check your reach while climbing: Record which hand position you use on the climb. On a quiet, safe section, check whether you can shift and brake from that position. You need to look ahead without letting go of the controls. If a brake lever is difficult to reach, check whether your model offers reach adjustment. Have it adjusted according to manufacturer instructions if needed, then check braking operation. Record the original setting; keep handlebar components within their clamping marks and respect specified torque values. Ride two to three easy trials: Use a familiar climb and change only one element at a time. Keep route and conditions as comparable as possible. Afterwards, record position, selected gear, perceived effort and any discomfort. Only then compare actual time with the estimate. Restore your previous setup if control or comfort worsens. Do not make the next ride harder simply to achieve the calculated power. Allow flexibility and recognise warnings: Avoid connections that depend on achieving the predicted time. Stop for pain or unsafe handling. Ask a fitter to review a persistent position problem. Pain at rest or at night, swelling and radiating tingling need medical assessment. If pain remains after three to four careful adjustments, seek help instead of continuing to experiment. Further reading What is cycling FTP? helps you assess which power value to enter and understand the uncertainty attached to it. Cycling power and speed: what changes? explains why the same effort can produce different speeds along your route. Mountain bike fit: control and movement helps you check position and control when your climb includes unpaved sections. Endurance bike fit: comfort over distance helps you consider the distance still remaining after the summit. The climb calculator makes assumptions visible so you can compare different route inputs deliberately. Frequently asked questions Does the displayed time include my breaks? No, the model calculates time from distance and estimated riding speed. Add room for stops yourself when planning. Allow for junctions and waiting too. A precise number on the screen does not mean your arrival is predictable to the nearest minute. Why does average gradient not match every section? An average summarises the whole climb. It can hide steep ramps and flatter sections. Look at the route profile alongside the input field. Your gearing needs to suit the sections you actually ride, rather than just the average shown in the calculator. Should I maintain the suggested power throughout? No. The power factor is a model choice based on distance. It is not an individual exercise test. Use experience and conditions to ride more gently whenever needed. Choosing a lower effort does not mean you have failed to follow the calculation correctly. Does a different saddle height predict a time saving? No, the calculator does not measure saddle height or predict its effects. Adjust only for a clear position or control question. Record the starting position and test carefully. Judge comfort and control rather than expecting a promised improvement on the clock.Estimate your climb time using your own inputs and use the result to prepare for a measured ride.Estimate your climb time

rows.article: The problem: choosing crank length Your new bike has different cranks from your previous one. You are unsure whether that difference matters. Perhaps the top of the pedal stroke feels cramped. Or you hear that shorter cranks automatically offer more comfort. It can be tempting to order another set immediately. First ask what you want to improve. Is it movement room, pedal clearance or a calculated size that differs? Record when you notice something and in which position. A symptom during a hard climb differs from feeling cramped in a low position. You can also be curious about another length without having symptoms. There is no need to rush. Record your current measurement and setup before comparing components. That prevents an expensive purchase from introducing several unknown changes together. This guide helps you prepare the discussion and any eventual test. Background: the pedal circle changes Crank length is the distance from the centre of the bottom bracket to the centre of the pedal axle. You do not measure to the end of the crank arm. The measurement is often marked on its inside. Check both sides if you are unsure about the components' history. A shorter arm describes a smaller circle. With the saddle unchanged, this alters the distance to the pedal along its path. The pedal reaches less high at the top and less low at the bottom. Crank length and saddle height therefore need consideration together. A change can also affect the perceived saddle-to-bar relationship when saddle height is adjusted. Shimano describes shorter cranks as one possible way to reduce the hip flexion required in a low position. That provides a reason for focused testing, not a guarantee that a particular symptom will disappear. The same source describes testing in 2.5 mm increments on a fitting bike; available lengths differ between crank models. Body measurements help establish a starting point. They cannot describe how you move or which position you sustain comfortably. Shoes, pedals and intended riding also belong in the assessment. A result with a precise number remains advice with limitations. The replacement also needs to fit mechanically. Consider the bottom bracket, chainline, chainrings and any power meter. Length alone cannot establish compatibility. Check combinations with the manufacturer or mechanic before buying. A suitable measurement on paper does not guarantee a suitable installation. How to approach it with bike fitting Read your existing measurement: Find the length marking on the inside of the crank arm. If it is unreadable, measure centre to centre with an accurate ruler. Record millimetres, brand and model. Do not measure along the sloping outer edge. Take a photograph so a fitter or mechanic knows which component you mean. Measure your inseam again: Follow the measurement instructions in the crank length calculator. Use the same position when repeating the measurement and ask for help if reading it is difficult. Also record the type of bike involved. A result that differs from your current length invites comparison, not immediate replacement. Define what you will compare: Describe your aim: room at the top, comfortable pedalling or position under load. Record saddle height, setback and handlebar position using fixed reference points. Keep symptom notes separately. Have existing pain assessed before treating a crank change as a remedy. A calculator cannot establish its cause. Plan one controlled comparison: Discuss an available alternative length with a fitter, preferably on an adjustable fitting bike. A 2.5 mm step is a described testing option, not a mandatory correction for every rider. Have the corresponding saddle position checked too. Record all necessary corrections as one test setup so the comparison remains clear. Check mechanics and riding feel: Have components installed according to the correct manual and check any power meter setting. If position-related pain persists after three to four careful adjustments, seek guidance instead of repeatedly buying components. Do not wait through those tests when sensation is reduced. h1: Cycling fueling basics: build a practical plan
rows.quick: Quick answerCycling fueling basics works best as a simple plan you can execute safely on the road. Choose familiar products, include carbohydrate from drinks and keep food accessible. Start with expected duration, practise on easy rides and change one element at a time; a complicated schedule helps little if packaging is difficult to open or your stomach objects.
rows.article: The problem: cycling fueling basics Before leaving you hurriedly put something in a pocket. An hour later it remains there because the pace is high or the packaging is awkward. At the first stop you eat a lot at once. Another day you have a schedule but not the products required to follow it. This guide mainly concerns execution. How do you carry food, when can you reach it safely and what should you record afterwards? The hourly calculation is useful, but not the whole story. A plan must match the route, your handling skills and your experience with the chosen products. Consider what already works well too. Perhaps an ordinary snack feels comfortable during easy rides. That is useful information, not a reason to replace everything immediately with sports products. Start with something repeatable and define which part of the plan you want to improve on your next outing. Background Preparation involves several choices: duration, expected effort, available stops and carrying capacity. These connect without needing to become a complicated formula. Write them down beforehand. This avoids discovering halfway through a ride that bottles are empty and the next shop is closed, or that food cannot be reached easily. The calculator uses duration categories from the approved carbohydrate guidance in Jeukendrup 2014. Its result is a starting point rather than an assessment of your complete diet. The explanation for short and long rides accompanies the number. Consider it when preparing a different type of effort. Food and fluid are not identical needs, even when one bottle provides both. Carbohydrate in drinks contributes to nutrition. Fluid quantity needs separate consideration alongside that. Wanting to carry more energy does not automatically justify mixing an arbitrarily stronger drink than the product instructions recommend for preparation and use. The bicycle arrangement affects execution. An inaccessible rear pocket, difficult bottle or tense hand position makes eating less practical. Check access while safely stationary. You do not need to struggle with a packet while riding to demonstrate that you are taking nutrition seriously or following a worthwhile plan. A successful ride provides information even when you do not consume everything. Record leftover food and why it remained unused. Was the ride shorter, did the product feel uncomfortable, or were safe opportunities lacking? Those answers help more than concluding afterwards that you lacked discipline because supplies remained in your pocket. How to approach it Choose a familiar route and estimate actual duration. Record places to stop, refill water or eat safely. Use the nutrition tool to examine a starting point. Read its limitations. Do not assume identical supplies suit a short easy outing and a much longer ride with limited facilities or opportunities to obtain more food. Lay out your chosen products before leaving. Check the label for carbohydrate in each actual serving. Count drinks when they contain carbohydrate too. Record your total and planned hours. Prefer an understandable combination over several unfamiliar products whose tolerance you have never tested during a ride or similar training session. Make food accessible. Distribute packets among pockets you can identify easily and secure them properly. Check while stationary that bottles leave their cages comfortably. Keep sharp or dangling packaging away from moving parts. If reaching requires a large twist, choose another location or plan a short stop rather than struggling while riding. Choose a simple rhythm suited to clear sections of the route. A reminder may help, but must not force an unsafe eating moment. Pause when braking, traffic or terrain requires attention. Keep both hands available whenever necessary; safety takes priority over completing the plan at an exact time shown on a device. Test two or three easy rides using the same base plan. Then change one product, quantity or carrying arrangement. Record stomach comfort, ease of eating and leftovers. Return to the previous approach if the new one feels worse. Avoid simultaneously changing your whole bike position or training load, because that mixes several possible explanations. Discuss persistent nutrition difficulties with a sports dietitian or clinician. Stop for serious illness, confusion or persistent vomiting. Pain at rest, night pain, swelling or radiating tingling needs medical assessment. Have posture symptoms reviewed after three or four careful adjustments; do not continue a fitting trial simply because you still have food left to consume. Further reading Carbs per hour cycling: make your plan helps interpret labels and add food and drink together for your planned outing. Sodium cycling drink: read the concentration explains what sodium information you can obtain from a product label. Cycling watts per kilogram: understand the number puts effort beside the figures used to describe your training. The fuel and hydration calculator provides a starting point to combine with your own experience and safe route planning, rather than replacing either. Frequently asked questions Do I need gels for every ride? No. Choice depends on duration, practical opportunities and tolerance. A gel is a packaging format, not a compulsory part of cycling. First consider guidance for the ride and products you already enjoy using. Practise new choices during an easy training session rather than an important event. What if a planned eating moment is unsafe? Delay it until a clear section or stop briefly. A reminder on a cycling computer is not an instruction to open packaging in traffic or on difficult terrain. Include that constraint in route planning, so safe opportunities are part of preparation instead of something you hope to find. Must I eat everything I carried? No. Preparation does not oblige you to empty your supplies. The ride may unfold differently from expectations. Record leftovers and the reason so you can plan better next time. Do not force intake when symptoms appear simply because a calculator displayed a particular amount before you left. Is an indoor trainer useful for practising eating? It can help assess access and tolerance under calm conditions. Keep drinks and packaging safely clear of moving parts. Indoor riding does not reproduce outdoor steering and traffic situations, however. sections.title: The problem: cycling fueling basics
sections.text: Before leaving you hurriedly put something in a pocket. An hour later it remains there because the pace is high or the packaging is awkward. At the first stop you eat a lot at once. Another day you have a schedule but not the products required to follow it. This guide mainly concerns execution. How do you carry food, when can you reach it safely and what should you record afterwards? The hourly calculation is useful, but not the whole story. A plan must match the route, your handling skills and your experience with the chosen products. Consider what already works well too. Perhaps an ordinary snack feels comfortable during easy rides. That is useful information, not a reason to replace everything immediately with sports products. Start with something repeatable and define which part of the plan you want to improve on your next outing.

sections.title: Background
sections.text: Preparation involves several choices: duration, expected effort, available stops and carrying capacity. These connect without needing to become a complicated formula. Write them down beforehand. This avoids discovering halfway through a ride that bottles are empty and the next shop is closed, or that food cannot be reached easily. The calculator uses duration categories from the approved carbohydrate guidance in Jeukendrup 2014. Its result is a starting point rather than an assessment of your complete diet. The explanation for short and long rides accompanies the number. Consider it when preparing a different type of effort. Food and fluid are not identical needs, even when one bottle provides both. Carbohydrate in drinks contributes to nutrition. Fluid quantity needs separate consideration alongside that. Wanting to carry more energy does not automatically justify mixing an arbitrarily stronger drink than the product instructions recommend for preparation and use. The bicycle arrangement affects execution. An inaccessible rear pocket, difficult bottle or tense hand position makes eating less practical. Check access while safely stationary. You do not need to struggle with a packet while riding to demonstrate that you are taking nutrition seriously or following a worthwhile plan. A successful ride provides information even when you do not consume everything. Record leftover food and why it remained unused. Was the ride shorter, did the product feel uncomfortable, or were safe opportunities lacking? Those answers help more than concluding afterwards that you lacked discipline because supplies remained in your pocket.

sections.title: How to approach it
sections.text: Choose a familiar route and estimate actual duration. Record places to stop, refill water or eat safely. Use the nutrition tool to examine a starting point. Read its limitations. Do not assume identical supplies suit a short easy outing and a much longer ride with limited facilities or opportunities to obtain more food. Lay out your chosen products before leaving. Check the label for carbohydrate in each actual serving. Count drinks when they contain carbohydrate too. Record your total and planned hours. Prefer an understandable combination over several unfamiliar products whose tolerance you have never tested during a ride or similar training session. Make food accessible. Distribute packets among pockets you can identify easily and secure them properly. Check while stationary that bottles leave their cages comfortably. Keep sharp or dangling packaging away from moving parts. If reaching requires a large twist, choose another location or plan a short stop rather than struggling while riding. Choose a simple rhythm suited to clear sections of the route. A reminder may help, but must not force an unsafe eating moment. Pause when braking, traffic or terrain requires attention. Keep both hands available whenever necessary; safety takes priority over completing the plan at an exact time shown on a device. Test two or three easy rides using the same base plan. Then change one product, quantity or carrying arrangement. Record stomach comfort, ease of eating and leftovers. Return to the previous approach if the new one feels worse. Avoid simultaneously changing your whole bike position or training load, because that mixes several possible explanations. Discuss persistent nutrition difficulties with a sports dietitian or clinician. Stop for serious illness, confusion or persistent vomiting. Pain at rest, night pain, swelling or radiating tingling needs medical assessment. Have posture symptoms reviewed after three or four careful adjustments; do not continue a fitting trial simply because you still have food left to consume.

rows.quick: Quick answerCycling shoe width cannot be solved simply by choosing a longer size. Compare the forefoot, heel and space above the instep separately to find a suitable shape. rows.article: The problem: cycling shoe width Your toes do not reach the front, but the shoe presses along your forefoot. Or you choose a roomier size and then notice your heel moving. Sometimes only the upper feels restrictive, while there seems to be enough space beside the foot. The size number tells only part of the story. You may not notice this immediately when trying shoes on. During a longer ride, you want to loosen the closure. Thicker socks change how the same shoe feels. Switching insoles may instead create more pressure over the instep. Write down where you lack space and where your foot moves. Assess left and right separately. Record the socks, insole and closure setting as well. This makes comparisons between models much clearer. You are not simply looking for the widest shoe. You need a shape that holds your foot without squeezing it locally. Address that question before moving your cleats. Background: length, last shape and internal space differ A last is the shape around which a shoe is made. Two models bearing the same size number can therefore feel different. Length describes space along the shoe, but does not automatically describe the shape around the forefoot, heel or instep. Shimano's shoe fitting guidance explains that width and internal volume should be assessed alongside length. A wider version can therefore solve a different problem from a longer shoe. This is a reason to compare shapes, not a guarantee that one label will fit your foot. Tracing your foot on paper gives useful information, but not a complete fit assessment. The outline does not show how much space you need above the foot, for example. Seams and closures can also sit in different places. Alongside your measurements, record where you actually feel pressure. An insole is another part of the available space. Adding a thicker one changes more than what sits underneath your foot. It also changes where the foot sits inside the shoe. An insole is therefore not an independent solution for every pressure point. A cleat changes the connection to the pedal, not the internal shape of the shoe. Adjusting cleats first makes little sense when the shoe already pinches before clipping in. Conversely, a good shoe fit can coexist with an uncomfortable pedal position. Online tools can compare measurements and prepare questions. They cannot reliably feel where a shoe presses under load. A fitting appointment helps when length, width and security never seem satisfactory together. How to approach it with bike fitting Describe the problem before buying. Record the precise location: little toe, ball of the foot, heel or instep. Note when it begins. Compare walking and other shoes. Pain away from cycling deserves a broader assessment than simply trying another bicycle model or shoe size. Measure both feet in millimetres. Use paper, a pencil and a ruler. Follow the measurement method of the brand you want to compare. Record foot length and the widest part of the forefoot. Repeat in the same stance. An accidental difference between two drawings is not yet a difference between your feet. Compare shapes before closures. Bring your usual cycling socks and insoles to a fitting appointment. Where available, compare different last widths at a suitable length. Check that your toes can rest naturally and your heel stays sufficiently secure. Avoid a universal millimetre rule for toe space when the brand provides its own fitting guidance. Change one component at a time. Compare another shoe without simultaneously adding a new insole or thicker socks. Record the model, size and width label. Tighten the closure only enough to hold the shoe securely. More tension is not a useful test when it immediately creates a pressure point. Check the pedal connection again. Mounting points and markings may differ with other shoes. Do not copy the old cleat position blindly. Have installation checked and practise safe engagement and release. The bike fit calculator offers a general starting point for your riding position, but cannot select a suitable shoe last. Compare in easy conditions. Test a safe, suitable combination over two to three easy rides. Keep other adjustments unchanged and note when discomfort begins. Stop if the shoe pinches or you lose sensation. Return to the previous comfortable combination rather than trying to make pain part of the adjustment process. Warning signs: numbness and spreading tingling are reasons not to keep riding. Have swelling or pain at rest or at night medically assessed. Seek a fitter and medical advice where appropriate if pain remains after three to four careful adjustments. A foot that already hurts away from cycling does not need that whole sequence first.
